Assumptions and cautions
- Medical clearance: OB cleared for moderate exercise; no jumping for the first 4 weeks post-clearance. Monitor for diastasis recti (DR), pelvic floor heaviness, leakage, or unusual pain. If any red flags, regress and consult.

- Training frequency: 4 days/week (mon/wed/fri/sat or as available). Each session includes warm-up, main work, and cooldown.
- Progression principle: Week 1 emphasis on technique, Week 2 increase reps/sets slightly, Week 3 introduce mild loading progression, Week 4 cap with slightly higher effort but still no impact/pounding.

Week 1 – Acclimatisation (Light, technique-focused)
Goal: Reconnect with breath-work, pelvic floor activation, hip hinge mechanics, and establish baseline movement quality. No jumping, no heavy loading.

Session A (Full-body, no impact)

  - 2 minutes dynamic hip circles, leg swings (supportive)
  - 3 minutes thoracic spine rotation and scapular mobility

Good question. Diastasis recti (DRA) can be subtle postpartum and some clients haven’t had formal screening. A practical, clinician-friendly approach is to screen safely as you progress the program, and to track signs that might indicate DRA is present or worsened. Here’s a concise guideline you can follow with your client, plus how to interpret findings and adapt your plan.

What to screen for (key indicators)
- Abdominal separation: measure at the midline just above and below the umbilicus when the client performs a small abdominal curl or head/shoulder lift.
  - Normal (no DRA): a single finger or 1–2 cm gap at rest or with light contraction.
  - Possible DRA: a gap that is 2 cm or greater (about two finger widths or more) that remains or widens with gentle contraction.
- Palpable doming or “mushiness” along the linea alba when bracing, or with a cough, Valsalva, or gentle crunching.
- Core function signs:
  - Excessive rib flare or lower back arch when attempting abdominal bracing.
  - Pelvic floor symptoms in conjunction with abdominal load (urge leakage, heaviness, bulge in midline).
  - Inability to maintain core bracing while performing loaded or anti-flexion movements.
- Functional symptoms:
  - Pain with certain activities (rolling to the side, sit-ups initially, bending/lifting) that aren’t typical for her.
  - Perception of abdominal instability during core tasks.

How to perform a simple, clinical self-check (safe approach)
- Position: client lies on their back with knees bent (hook-lying) and feet flat. For mild DR, lying with head supported is fine; for more accurate assessment, a supine check is common.
- Locate the linea alba: place two fingers horizontally about an inch above and below the belly button, along the midline.
- Perform a small abdominal contraction (gentle head/shoulders lift or a “crunch” very lightly). The client should feel the deep core, not the rectus doming.
- Observe: with a light isometric contraction, does the gap widen, stay the same, or narrow? Also note any doming or bulge along the midline.
- Repeat in different positions:
  - Fully supine (knee bent) and then in a tall kneeling position with a gentle brace.
  - If safe, check in a dead bug position (opposite arm/leg reach) to see if the midline stays stable.
- Documentation: record the distance if possible (in finger widths or cm) at rest and during light contraction, and note doming presence.

Formal vs pragmatic approaches
- Formal clinical assessment (via palpation) is best done by a qualified clinician (physio/physiotherapist, OB PT, or pelvic health PT). If available, schedule a formal assessment around week 6–8 postpartum or at the next postpartum check.
- In the absence of formal testing, use a repeated, standardized, gentle self-check during the program, at consistent points (e.g., Weeks 2, 4, and 6). Track changes in symptoms and palpation findings rather than relying solely on a numerical measurement.

How to adapt training based on findings
- If no or mild DRA:
  - Continue with the on-ramp plan, prioritizing braced maneuvers, anti-flexion work, and intra-abdominal pressure control.
  - Continue to progress load gradually; monitor for doming or leakage during loaded core tasks.
- If moderate-to-severe DRA or increasing dome/instability:
  - Maintain safer progressions, emphasize transverse abdominis bracing with diaphragmatic breathing.
  - Avoid activities that provoke significant midline separation during the early weeks (e.g., full sit-ups, full crunches, high loaded anti-flexion with hard brace).
  - Prefer anti-flexion core moves, isometric holds, and anti-rotation work with proper bracing.
  - Consider consulting a pelvic health PT for a targeted program and assessment.
- If symptoms (pelvic girdle, leakage, heaviness) worsen:
  - Scale back to lower-load variations, reduce range of motion in flexion-based movements, and re-check bracing technique.
  - Reassess after 1–2 weeks; if no improvement, escalate to formal screening.

Practical screening plan integrated into your 4-week on-ramp
- Week 1: baseline self-checks during your initial warm-up or core block; note any doming or gaps. No changes to plan unless red flags appear.
- Week 3: repeat the midline check in 2–3 positions (supine, tall kneeling, and a controlled dead bug stance) and compare with Week 1. Use this to guide any minor modifications.
- Week 6 (post 4-week ramp and re-check): if possible, arrange a formal screening with a pelvic health PT. If not, perform the same unit checks and bring in a more conservative approach if any widening or doming appears.
- Documentation: maintain a simple log. Record DR status (none/mild/moderate), any doming observed, presence of leakage, and the client’s subjective sense of core stability during workouts.

Communication cues for the client
- Normalize: many postpartum clients have some degree of diastasis that improves with time and proper rehab.
- Reassure: focus on safe progression and core bracing rather than chasing a perfect measurement.
- Encourage reporting: any new or worsened abdominal bulge, leakage, pain, or heaviness should be reported immediately so you can adjust.

What else helps
- Pelvic floor strategy: continue Kegels or pelvic floor activation as appropriate, integrated with diaphragmatic breathing during each exercise.
- Breathing pattern: inhale to diaphragmatic expansion; exhale-brace during exertion in core and lifting movements.
- Exercise substitutions: if a movement provokes doming, substitute with a safer anti-flexion or anti-rotation variant (e.g., Pallof press, dead bug, anti-rotation carries).

Here’s a concise, at-a-glance summary of the 4-week return-to-fitness plan, plus what to screen for each week. It combines the on-ramp, cardio/HIIT, anti-flexion core work, and the early-running considerations we discussed.

Overall structure
- Frequency: 4 training days per week
  - 2 strength days with integrated anti-flexion core work
  - 2 cardio/HIIT days (non-jumping, low impact)
- Jumping: remain non-jumping for the full 4 weeks
- Progression: increase in small steps (load, tempo, volume) only if technique and core/pelvic floor control stay solid
- Screening: ongoing diastasis/pelvic-floor/brace monitoring and red flags

Week 1 — Acclimatisation and technique focus
What it looks like
- Strength days: technique-first sessions with light loads; emphasis on pelvic floor engagement, diaphragmatic breathing, and anti-flexion core moves
- Cardio days: light, non-impact options (stationary bike, incline walking) for 10–12 minutes total
- Anti-flexion core: 2 sets per exercise across 4–5 moves (dead bug, supine march with brace, modified planks, Pallof press) integrated into the end of sessions
- Recovery: focus on sleep, protein intake, and hydration

What we screen for
- Pelvic-floor integrity during and after core work
- Absence of abdominal doming or midline bulge with bracing
- No new low-back or pelvic pain during or after workouts
- Comfort with the loaded movements (technique remains priority)

Week 2 — Light progression
What it looks like
- Strength: small loading increases if technique is solid; reps rise toward 10–12 with careful load
- Tempo: introduce a controlled eccentric (e.g., 3-second descent) on key lifts
- Cardio: extend to 12–15 minutes; optional one additional short interval
- Anti-flexion core: escalate to 3 sets for most moves; add a longer Pallof hold or an extra anti-rotation hold
- Cardio variety: keep non-impact modalities; consider a second cardio day if tolerated

What we screen for
- Consistency of bracing under heavier loads
- Any signs of doming or leakage under increased effort
- Fatigue management between sessions; ensure adequate recovery

Week 3 — Moderate loading and more volume
What it looks like
- Strength: 3 sets of 12–15 on most movements with light-to-moderate load; tempo continues to emphasize control (2–0–2 or 3–0–2)
- Cardio/HIIT: maintain 2 sessions, 18–25 minutes; 1 interval block with slightly longer work bouts if tolerated
- Anti-flexion core: 4 sets across 4–5 core moves; include standing anti-rotation or Pallof press with heavier resistance
- Running prep discussion begins later in week if tolerance remains positive (no impact yet)

What we screen for
- Ability to maintain brace with longer sets and heavier loads
- Any new symptoms with higher effort (leakage, heaviness, pain)
- Adequate recovery indicators (sleep, appetite, mood)

Week 4 — Peak on-ramp, consolidate safety
What it looks like
- Strength: sustain or slightly increase loads; 3 sets of 12–15 or 4 sets of ~10 where appropriate
- Cardio/HIIT: 2–3 sessions; intervals 1 minute at a comfortable but more challenging pace with 1–2 minutes easy
- Anti-flexion core: 4–5 sets across 4–5 moves; includes standing anti-extension holds
- Cool-downs: include mobility work and diaphragmatic breathing to promote recovery

What we screen for
- Diastasis status and midline control during higher loads
- Pelvic floor symptoms with cumulative fatigue
- Readiness to progress to running (if symptoms remain well-managed, running progression can be planned after this ramp)

Key safety cues throughout the 4 weeks
- Pelvic floor engagement before and during every movement
- Bracing the core without bearing down; avoid Valsalva especially during cardio
- Breathing: exhale on exertion, inhale on lowering/relaxation
- Progressions: only one variable at a time (load, tempo, volume)
- Red flags: new leakage, pelvic heaviness, sharp/persistent pelvic or back pain, or worsening DOMS beyond 48 hours—regress

What to track and document
- Core/pelvic-floor status (doming, leakage, heaviness)
- Perceived exertion (RPE) and breathing quality
- Weekly loads, reps, tempo notes
- Sleep, appetite, and overall recovery
- Any symptoms during or after cardio/HIIT (for ongoing safety)

- I can also append a simple diastasis/self-screening checklist to use weekly (Week 1, Week 3, Week 4).
